assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened moire quantum materials: a tunable platform for correlated insulators, superconductivity and orbital magnetism, born from a quantitative continuum-model prediction of flat bands near a specific twist angle. It is the kind of surprise from a two-dimensional crystal that I value, with theory and experiment tightly linked.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the flat-band prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group (with Cao and colleagues) measured the correlated and superconducting states. This gives a clean theory plus experiment split in three. Other contributors (e.g. the early Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto work, and Cao as lead experimentalist) are not on the credited list, so I would want to examine how that is handled.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many independent groups across several platforms since 2018; the single-particle theory is robust. Recognition is timely, though the mechanism of the superconductivity and the correlated phases is still debated.
uncertainties: Origin of superconductivity in twisted graphene is unresolved; the prize would reward the platform and flat-band prediction rather than a final mechanism.
Credit for earlier theory of twisted-bilayer band structure and for the lead experimental student is outside the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect revealed a new class of electronic states, with protected edge or surface states from band topology; the idea is original, general and now underlies a large part of materials physics. The link to first-principles band-structure calculations and ARPES spectroscopy is strong, which suits my own perspective.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical proposal (Z2 invariant, quantum spin Hall in graphene); Molenkamp's group observed the effect in HgTe quantum wells after the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore, Balents, and Hasan, who demonstrated 3D topological insulators, are not in this credited set, so the configuration omits important contributors and is only one fair reading.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and Bi-based 3D materials, with spectroscopic verification. Over fifteen years of consolidation; recognition is arguably overdue, though the Thouless/Haldane/Kosterlitz prize in 2016 touched the topic.
uncertainties: Priority questions around BHZ, Fu-Kane-Mele and Moore-Balents, and the experimental 3D discovery by Hasan's group, could make a three-person split contentious.
Overlap with candidate B012 (same field) means the committee would need to choose one framing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magnetic skyrmions are topologically protected spin textures observed in real and reciprocal space, with a direct connection to my own work on magnetic interactions and atomistic spin dynamics (Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, spin-lattice simulations). The discovery is clear and the potential for spintronics is real, though still largely prospective.
assessment.attribution: Pfleiderer's group (with Muhlbauer, Boni) found the skyrmion lattice in MnSi; Tokura's group imaged it in real space in FeCoSi; Wiesendanger's group demonstrated atomic-scale skyrmions at an interface. Theoretical predictions by Bogdanov, Rossler and others are not in the credited set, and this is an important missing piece.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many neutron, Lorentz-TEM and spin-polarized STM studies, with theory reproducing the stability. Applications such as racetrack memory remain unproven, so recognition rests on fundamental discovery.
uncertainties: Missing credit for the theoretical prediction (Bogdanov and collaborators) makes the three-person configuration debatable.
Technological relevance is not yet demonstrated, which may count against timeliness.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is the first controllable framework for strongly correlated electrons, giving a quantitative description of Mott transitions and, combined with DFT (LDA+DMFT), predictions of real materials spectra. Its importance for materials theory and for interpreting photoemission is substantial, and as a first-principles theorist I recognize how much it changed practice.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt introduced the infinite-dimension limit; Georges and Kotliar established the mapping to an impurity problem; Kotliar and Vollhardt developed the materials-oriented extension. Metzner, Muller-Hartmann, Rozenberg and Jarrell also made decisive contributions that are not on the supplied list.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with many independent implementations and agreement with experiment in several materials. Quantitative accuracy depends on approximations (double counting, impurity solvers), which tempers confidence.
uncertainties: Credit is spread over a larger community than three names can cover.
Prize committees have tended to favor discoveries over methods, and I am unsure of the appetite here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Giant tunnel magnetoresistance in MgO-based magnetic tunnel junctions made spintronic read heads and magnetic random-access memory practical. It rests on a physical mechanism, coherent spin-dependent tunneling, that was predicted by ab initio calculation and then confirmed by experiment, which is exactly the theory-to-measurement path I value.
assessment.attribution: Butler's first-principles prediction of large TMR in Fe/MgO/Fe, followed by the Parkin and Yuasa experiments in 2004, supports a fair three-person set. Miyazaki and Moodera (room-temperature TMR in 1995) are important too, and Mathon and Umerski also predicted it; the fourth credited name is left out only because of the three-laureate limit.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed and industrially deployed, so maturity is high. The Nobel Prize for GMR (2007) lowers the novelty for some, which could weigh against it.
uncertainties: Relative standing versus the 2007 GMR prize and the earlier Miyazaki/Moodera discovery.
The device engineering component may be seen as more technology than physics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological order and long-range entanglement offer a conceptual framework for phases beyond Landau symmetry breaking, linking fractional quantum Hall physics, spin liquids and quantum error correction. The originality is high and the influence on condensed-matter theory is large.
assessment.attribution: Wen introduced topological order in the late 1980s and Kitaev's toric-code and anyon work (2003) added the exactly solvable models; two names are a natural pair. Others, e.g. Read, Moore, Levin and Hastings, are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Theory is widely accepted, but direct experimental verification of topological order in real materials is incomplete and quantum simulators are only beginning to realize it. I would defer for confirmation.
uncertainties: Few unambiguous experimental realizations; claims of spin liquids in materials remain contested.
Kitaev also appears in the error-correction candidate, so double recognition would need thought.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks gave a roughly hundredfold improvement in timekeeping precision, relying on the magic-wavelength idea and many-body control; they enable tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy. The result is clear and precisely measured, though I lean on colleagues for deep assessment of atomic physics.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice; Ye's group demonstrated record stability and many-body effects in strontium. Hall and Hansch were already recognized for the frequency comb in 2005, and Ludlow and others contributed, but a two-person award looks fair.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation across several laboratories and species; measurements are stable and progress is continuing, so timeliness is good.
uncertainties: Overlap with the earlier 2012 and 2005 prizes in precision metrology.
I defer to AMO members on the relative merit of ion clocks versus lattice clocks (credit is not fully settled).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Spin Hall and inverse spin Hall effects convert charge into spin current and back, underpinning spin-orbit torque devices and electrical detection of spin currents. It is a clearly physical discovery in a field close to mine, with connections to relativistic band-structure theory.
assessment.attribution: Dyakonov and Perel made the original prediction (1971); Awschalom's group made the first optical observation in semiconductors (2004); Saitoh's group demonstrated the inverse effect and spin pumping in metals. Jungwirth, Hirsch, Zhang, and Kato are also tied to it, so the choice among four named is a judgment call and Hirsch is absent.
assessment.maturity: The effects are very well confirmed, but the observation history is complicated by multiple independent approaches and extrinsic versus intrinsic mechanisms.
uncertainties: Priority and credit disputes (Hirsch, Zhang, Murakami-Nagaosa-Zhang, Sinova) are considerable.
Overlap with the GMR and TMR candidates; the committee may regard spintronics as already honored.
